lessons.unit: Unit 1: Respectful relationships and online safety
lessons.title: Healthy and unhealthy relationships: respect, boundaries and consent
objectives: Explain consent as freely given, informed and able to be withdrawn, in everyday situations
Recognise controlling behaviour and pressure in relationships
Link respect, modesty (haya) and dignity to healthy relationships and know where to get help

keywords.def: freely given agreement that can be withdrawn at any time
pressuring or forcing someone to do something
trying to dominate what another person does or feels
modesty and a sense of shame about what is wrong
the right to be respected and valued

starter: Bismillah. Name two features of a healthy friendship.
Give an assertive phrase for refusing something.

teach.heading: Healthy relationships
bullets: You feel safe and free to be yourself
Applies to family, friends and online contacts
teach.note: Say bismillah. Explain that this lesson is about friendships, family and online contacts (in Islam, romantic relationships belong only within marriage), and is taught within the TGA RSHE Policy. Parents have been informed of the content. Revisit key features of healthy relationships. Link to Qur'an 30:21, which describes love and mercy between spouses as a sign from Allah, and to the hadith that the best of you are the best to their families (Tirmidhi). Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Integrity. Taught to boys and girls separately. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Consent in everyday life
bullets: Silence or fear is not consent
You can change your mind any time
Applies to touch, photos, secrets and belongings
teach.note: Begin with low-risk examples: borrowing a phone, hugging someone, taking and sharing a photo, reading private messages. Teach that consent must be freely given, informed and specific. Misconception: if someone did not say no, it is fine. Emphasise that we must stop and check if someone seems uncertain. Do not discuss sexual detail. Explain that the same principles apply in every relationship.

teach.heading: Pressure, coercion and control
bullets: Checking your phone or tracking you
Cutting you off from friends and family
Humiliation, jealousy and anger used to control
teach.note: Use invented case studies of friendships and online contacts rather than romantic ones. Examples: a friend threatens to share a secret if you don't do what they say; an older contact flatters a pupil and asks them to keep their chats secret. Ask pupils to identify the red flags. Explain that anyone can experience coercive behaviour, and it is never the victim's fault.

teach.heading: Values: haya, dignity and the law
bullets: Qur'an 24:30: lower the gaze and guard modesty
Hadith: modesty is part of faith
UK law protects young people; the age of consent is 16
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 24:30 commands believers to lower their gaze and guard their modesty, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught that modesty is part of faith (Bukhari and Muslim). Explain that Islamic teaching places intimate relationships within marriage, and that the law in the UK also sets an age of consent to protect young people. Keep to the facts; do not discuss details. If pupils ask questions, redirect to the question box and speak to the PSHE Lead.

teach.heading: Getting help
bullets: Tell a trusted adult or the DSL
teach.note: Make sure all pupils know the routes for help. Emphasise that no one will be blamed for reporting. Model what to say: ‘Something is happening that I'm not comfortable with and I need help.’ Explain that adults will take concerns seriously and act in the pupil's best interests. If a pupil discloses something during the lesson, follow safeguarding procedures and speak to the DSL the same day.

practice: Consent or not? (a) A friend says ‘ok’ after you keep asking five times. (b) A pupil says ‘yes, you can take the photo’ and later says ‘please delete it’. Explain each.
List three red flags of controlling behaviour.
Write two assertive sentences that set a boundary about sharing your phone.
independent: Write a short case study of an unhealthy friendship and how a pupil seeks help.
Create a poster: ‘Consent is…’ with five key points and a quotation from the lesson.
Write a paragraph explaining how haya and respect protect dignity.
exit: Name two places to get help.
lessons.homework: Talk with a trusted adult about what respect looks like in a family relationship and write four sentences about their view.
lessons.send: SEND: provide scenario cards with traffic-light responses and sentence frames. EAL: pre-teach ‘consent’, ‘coercion’ and ‘boundary’. Stretch: compare the idea of consent in UK law with Islamic ethical principles of respect and choice.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Respectful relationships and online safety
lessons.title: Sharing images and harmful content online
objectives: Explain the law and risks relating to nude or sexual images of under-18s
Describe how to respond to pressure, blackmail or harmful content and where to report
Evaluate misleading, extreme and sexually explicit content and why it is harmful

keywords.def: a nude or sexual image of a person
threatening to share something unless a person does what is demanded
false or misleading information
being drawn into extreme beliefs
a trust we must protect

starter: Bismillah. What is a digital footprint?
Name two places to report an online problem.

teach.heading: Online risks
teach.note: Say bismillah. Teach this lesson factually, without graphic detail, in line with the TGA RSHE Policy and Online Safety and Acceptable Use Policy. Parents have been informed. Explain the aim: to prepare pupils so that they can protect themselves and others. Reassure pupils that no one will be blamed if they ask for help. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Integrity and amanah. Taught to boys and girls separately. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Images and the law
bullets: It is illegal to take, share or keep nude images of under-18s
Once sent, you lose control of it
Police focus on protecting young people
teach.note: State facts: in UK law a nude or sexual image of anyone under 18 is treated as an indecent image of a child. This applies even when a young person creates it themselves. The police have said they focus on safeguarding, not criminalising young people. Teach that images can be copied, shared and used to hurt. Link to the hadith that whoever conceals the fault of a Muslim, Allah will conceal him in this world and the next (Muslim).

teach.heading: Pressure and blackmail
bullets: Stop contact and do not send more
Do not pay, and do not delete evidence
Tell a trusted adult; report to CEOP
teach.note: Explain that some people trick young people using fake profiles, flattery and then threats. Teach the steps: stop, save evidence, block, tell. Report Remove (Childline and the Internet Watch Foundation) can help get images taken down. Stress that adults will help without judgement. Role-play an invented chat in which a pupil receives pressure and chooses to tell an adult. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Resilience.

teach.heading: Harmful content
bullets: It can harm self-image and relationships
Extremist content uses emotion to recruit
teach.note: Keep this brief and non-graphic. Explain that pornography is harmful and haram: it is unrealistic, can become a habit that is hard to break, and distorts how people see themselves and others; Qur'an 24:30-31 commands believers to lower their gaze. Anyone who has seen it should not feel trapped: close it, turn to Allah in repentance and talk to a trusted adult. Explain that extremist groups may target young people online with simple answers and a sense of belonging. Cite plainly: Qur'an 49:6, to verify information before acting on it. Teach lateral reading: check who made it and what other trusted sources say. Refer to the Prevent policy for concerns.

teach.heading: What to do
bullets: Close the page, do not share it
Report to the DSL, platform, CEOP, Childline
teach.note: Summarise the key steps: close, tell, report. Explain that platforms have age restrictions and parents can set filters. Encourage pupils to build habits: ask whether it is true, kind and necessary before sharing. Close with a reminder that help is always available.

practice: True or false? (a) If you send a picture of yourself it cannot be illegal. (b) Blackmail is never your fault. (c) Report Remove can help get images taken down.
List the steps to take if someone pressures you to send a picture.
How can you check whether a shocking video is true?
independent: Create a flowchart: ‘I have received a worrying message, what do I do?’
Write a short dialogue showing a pupil telling a trusted adult about online pressure.
Write a paragraph on how amanah and haya protect us online.
exit: Why is it dangerous to share nude images of under-18s?
Give two steps to take if you are being blackmailed.
lessons.homework: Find out how to set up parental controls or filters on one device with a parent or carer, and write three sentences about what you learned.
lessons.send: SEND: provide flowchart templates and visual steps. EAL: pre-teach legal vocabulary. Stretch: research how the Online Safety Act 2023 requires platforms to protect children.

lessons.title: Earning and income: payslips, tax and National Insurance
lessons.bigQuestion: A job advert says £24,000 a year. Will you actually receive £24,000?
objectives: To understand how earnings become take-home pay after tax and National Insurance
successCriteria: All: explain gross pay, net pay and deductions
Most: read a payslip and find the deductions
Some: calculate basic-rate income tax and National Insurance on a salary
lessons.smsc: Social: how taxes fund public services we all use

keywords.def: pay before deductions
take-home pay after deductions
tax on earnings above the personal allowance
a payment from earnings that funds the state pension and benefits
the amount you can earn before paying income tax

hook.text: A job advert says £24,000 a year. Will you actually receive £24,000?
hook.a: No: income tax and National Insurance are taken first; take-home pay is less.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ praised earning by one's own hands (al-Bukhari) and Allah commands fulfilling contracts (al-Ma'idah 5:1). Honest work, honest pay and paying what the law requires are part of a Muslim's integrity.

starter.q: Name one thing taxes pay for.

starter.a: Interest on loans, forbidden in Islam.

teach.heading: Gross and net
bullets: Deductions: income tax, National Insurance, pension
teach.note: Payslip picture with no names.

teach.heading: Income tax and NI (2026-27, check gov.uk)
teach.note: Higher rates exist for higher earners; keep to basic rate here.

teach.heading: Model: take-home pay
bullets: Tax and NI on the taxable part
teach.note: Model.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: Net is what is left after tax, NI and other deductions.

practice.model: Teacher subtracts the personal allowance and explains no tax is paid on the first £12,570.

independent.q: Core: Payslip sheet (pupil PDF): find gross, each deduction and net pay on two payslips.
independent.a: Values read correctly from both payslips.

independent.q: Extend: Calculate take-home pay for a £30,000 salary (basic rate only).
Stretch: In the portal response box, explain why the tax system is called 'progressive'.
independent.a: People pay a higher share as income rises: allowance, then 20%, then higher rates.

exit.q: The personal allowance is... A) a bonus B) earnings you can receive before income tax C) a pension
exit.a: B) earnings you can receive before income tax

exit.q: Big question: will a £24,000 job pay you £24,000?
exit.a: No: about £20,800 after income tax and NI.

lessons.homework: With a parent's permission, look at a real or sample payslip and identify gross pay, deductions and net pay.
lessons.send: SEND: calculator and a partly worked example. EAL: gross, net, deduction. Stretch: research student loan repayments as a deduction.

lessons.title: Strengths and careers
lessons.bigQuestion: Should you choose a career for money, for passion, or for helping people? Can you have all three?
objectives: To understand how strengths, interests and values connect to future careers and Year 10 choices
successCriteria: All: name three personal strengths and interests
Most: link them to suitable careers and subjects
Some: research one career's route, training and how it serves the community
lessons.crossCurricular: All subjects: Year 10 option choices (two of Arabic, Business, Computer Science and Geography)

keywords.def: something you are good at
an ability you can learn and improve
the work a person does over their life
facts about jobs: demand, pay and growth

hook.text: Should you choose a career for money, for passion, or for helping people? Can you have all three?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'The best of people are those most beneficial to people' (at-Tabarani, graded hasan by al-Albani). Muslims seek halal work that benefits others, and every honest job done with good intention can be worship.

starter.a: Someone who lets criminals move money through their account.

teach.heading: Strengths and skills
teach.note: Examples: problem solving, communication, creativity, patience.

teach.heading: From strengths to careers
teach.note: Use the National Careers Service website (free, no login needed).

teach.heading: Model: researching a career
teach.note: Model.

steps: Role: prepares and advises on medicines
Route: A levels (chemistry), MPharm degree, foundation year
Pay and demand: check the National Careers Service profile
Benefit: keeps people safe and well

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which is a skill rather than an interest?
check.why: Typing is an ability that can be learned; the others are interests.

practice.q: Name one strength and one career it suits.
practice.model: Teacher shares their own strength and how it fits teaching.

independent.q: Core: Strengths audit (pupil PDF): list five strengths with evidence, then match three careers.
independent.a: Five evidenced strengths and three matched careers.
independent.model: Teacher completes the first strength with evidence.

independent.q: Extend: Research one career on the National Careers Service site and write a profile in the portal response box.
independent.a: Role, route, pay range, benefit to people.

independent.q: Stretch: Which two Year 10 options would help your chosen career? Explain.
independent.a: Options linked to the career with reasons.

exit.q: A skill is... A) something you can learn and improve B) only a hobby C) a salary
exit.a: A) something you can learn and improve
options: Something you can learn and improve

exit.q: Big question: money, passion or helping people: can you have all three?
exit.a: Often yes: choose halal work that uses your strengths and benefits others.

lessons.homework: Talk to an adult about their career: what strengths it needs and how they got there.
lessons.send: SEND: strengths word bank. EAL: strength, skill, career. Stretch: compare two career routes (degree and apprenticeship).

lessons.title: Budgeting
lessons.bigQuestion: Two people earn the same. One always runs out of money, one saves. What is the difference?
objectives: To understand how to build a monthly budget that covers needs, saving and giving
successCriteria: All: list fixed and variable costs
Most: build a balanced monthly budget
Some: adjust a budget after an unexpected cost and justify the choices
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentages and balancing totals; Computing: spreadsheets (Spring 2)

keywords.def: a plan for income and spending
a cost that stays the same each month, like rent
a cost that changes, like food
money left over
spending more than income

hook.text: Two people earn the same. One always runs out of money, one saves. What is the difference?

islamicLink.text: Allah praises those who, when they spend, are 'neither wasteful nor stingy, but in between' (al-Furqan 25:67), and warns that wasteful spenders are brothers of the devils (al-Isra 17:27). A budget puts this balance into practice, with zakah and sadaqah planned in.

starter.q: What does al-Furqan 25:67 teach about spending?
starter.a: Not wasteful nor stingy, in between.

teach.heading: Fixed and variable
bullets: Fixed: rent, council tax, phone contract
teach.note: Sort.

teach.heading: A simple budget
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Net income £1,700 a month. Rent £750, bills £250, food £300, travel £100.
model.answer: Balanced budget with giving and saving

teach.heading: When things change
bullets: Use the emergency fund, not riba debt
teach.note: This is why an emergency fund matters.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: Spending more than income is a deficit of £150.

practice.q: Income £1,200, needs £950. How much is left for saving, giving and wants?
practice.model: Teacher subtracts and suggests a split.

independent.q: Core: Budget task (pupil PDF): a young adult's monthly budget, balance it with saving and sadaqah.
independent.a: A balanced budget with needs first.

independent.q: Extend: A £200 car repair arrives. Adjust the budget and explain in the portal response box.
independent.a: Cut wants, use savings, avoid riba borrowing.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why an emergency fund helps a Muslim avoid riba.
independent.a: Savings cover surprises, so there is no need to borrow with interest.

exit.q: A fixed cost is... A) food B) rent C) a treat
Big question: same income, one saves and one runs out: why?
exit.a: Planning with a budget and spending wisely.

lessons.homework: List your own monthly spending (pocket money or imagined) as fixed and variable costs.
lessons.send: SEND: budget template with categories filled. EAL: fixed, variable, surplus, deficit. Stretch: build the budget in Excel (school Microsoft 365).

lessons.title: Saving, riba and halal ways to save
lessons.bigQuestion: If a bank offers you 4% interest on savings, is that a gift?
objectives: To understand why saving matters, why riba is forbidden, and how Muslims can save and grow money in halal ways
successCriteria: All: give three reasons to save
Most: explain how interest works and why Islam forbids riba
Some: compare halal options such as profit-sharing accounts and ethical investment
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentages and compound growth (taught as knowledge of the wider economy)
lessons.smsc: Moral and spiritual: obeying Allah in money matters

keywords.def: keeping money for the future
money paid for lending or borrowing money
interest, forbidden in Islam (رِبَا)
sharing real business profit and risk, as in mudarabah
savings kept for unexpected costs

hook.text: If a bank offers you 4% interest on savings, is that a gift?
hook.a: In Islam it is riba; Muslims choose halal alternatives that share real profit and risk.

islamicLink.text: Islamic note: riba (رِبَا) is forbidden (Qur'an 2:275: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba). Islamic finance uses partnership (mushārakah, مُشَارَكَة) and cost-plus sale (murābaḥah, مُرَابَحَة) instead. Allah says: 'Allah destroys riba and gives increase for charities' (al-Baqarah 2:276).

starter.q: Spending more than income is a...

teach.heading: Why save?
bullets: Big goals: hajj, a car, a home
teach.note: Zakah is due on savings above nisab held for a lunar year.

teach.heading: How interest works
teach.note: Knowledge of how the wider economy works, never as something to take.

teach.heading: Halal ways to save and grow
bullets: Current account or safe saving (no interest)
Partnership (musharakah) and cost-plus sale (murabahah) for buying
teach.note: Profit and risk are shared in real trade; no guaranteed return on money.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which is a halal way to grow savings?
options: A profit-sharing account based on real trade
check.why: Profit-sharing in real trade avoids riba; the others involve interest.

practice.q: Zakah on £8,000 savings held a lunar year above nisab?

independent.q: Core: Savings plan (pupil PDF): a goal, a monthly amount, and a halal place to keep it; include zakah if due.
independent.model: Teacher plans saving for a laptop.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, explain why Islam forbids riba. Start: 'Riba is forbidden because...'
independent.a: Riba is forbidden because Allah forbade it (2:275); it guarantees gain without shared risk and can trap the poor in debt.

independent.q: Stretch: Compare a profit-sharing account with an interest account: who carries the risk?
independent.a: Interest: the borrower; profit-sharing: shared between the bank and saver.

exit.q: Riba is... A) charity B) interest, forbidden in Islam C) zakah
Big question: is 4% interest a gift? What could a Muslim do instead?
exit.a: No, it is riba; use halal profit-sharing or keep savings safely.

lessons.homework: Ask a parent how your family saves and whether they use an Islamic bank account.
lessons.send: SEND: definitions card. EAL: saving, interest, profit. Stretch: research a UK Islamic bank's savings product.

lessons.title: Scams and staying safe with money
lessons.bigQuestion: Why would a scammer want to use a teenager's bank account?
objectives: To understand how money scams work and how to protect ourselves and our families
successCriteria: Most: spot the warning signs in a message or offer
Some: explain how to report a scam and help a vulnerable relative
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and protecting the vulnerable

keywords.def: a trick to steal money or information
a crime of deceiving people for money
someone who lets criminals move money through their account (a crime)
the UK's national reporting centre for fraud

hook.text: Why would a scammer want to use a teenager's bank account?
hook.a: To move stolen money (money mule). It is a crime, even if you only 'help'.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever cheats us is not one of us' (Muslim). Allah says: 'Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly' (an-Nisa 4:29). Protecting ourselves and others from fraud is part of justice.

starter.a: Urgency, odd links, asks for passwords.

teach.heading: Common scams
bullets: Fake online shops and too-good deals
teach.note: Use invented examples.

teach.heading: Warning signs
bullets: Asks for bank details or codes
Pay by bank transfer or gift card only
teach.note: Banks never ask for your full PIN or one-time code.

teach.heading: Money mules
bullets: Can mean a criminal record and losing your bank account
teach.note: Serious and common among young people.

teach.heading: What to do
bullets: Report: Action Fraud (actionfraud.police.uk) or 7726 for scam texts
Tell your bank at once if money is lost
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Text: 'Your parcel is held. Pay £1.45 here: bit.ly/xyz'
steps: Check: no parcel expected; the link is not the courier's site

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Someone online offers £300 to 'receive and send on' money through your account. This is...
check.why: It moves criminal money; the account holder can be prosecuted.

practice.q: Spot three warning signs: 'Congrats! You've won an iPhone. Pay £2 delivery in the next 10 minutes.'
practice.a: Unexpected prize, pressure (10 minutes), payment for a 'free' prize.

independent.q: Core: Scam or safe? (pupil PDF): judge eight messages and give a reason for each.
Extend: In the portal response box, write advice for an older relative about phone scams.
independent.a: Banks never ask for PINs; hang up and call the bank on a known number; tell family.

exit.q: To report a scam text in the UK, forward it to... A) 999 B) 7726 C) 111
Big question: why would a scammer want a teenager's bank account?
exit.a: To move stolen money (money mule), which is a crime.

lessons.homework: Show a family member the scam warning signs and the 7726 number.
lessons.send: SEND: warning signs checklist. EAL: scam, fraud, report. Stretch: research how banks refund authorised push payment fraud.
